clusters.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
clusters.neutral_headline: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers...

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
items.standfirst: Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything butWhen I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

clusters.title: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
clusters.neutral_headline: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey...

items.title: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
items.standfirst: Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choiceThe National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world.Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously, from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistThe Guardian’s year in review 2026 On Tuesday 1 December, join Guardian writers Zoe Williams, Lucy Mangan, Jonathan Liew, Heather Stewart, Pippa Crerar and John Crace for an evening of candid conversations as they look back on the year’s defining stories. Hosted by comedian Suzi Ruffell. Book tickets here or at guardian.live Continue reading...

items.standfirst: Measles is spreading across the world and could give rise to another pandemic, writes Colette McIvorAfter reading your report (‘They’re struggling for oxygen’: children pay the price as countries allow measles to surge again, 20 November), I was struck by the statement that proposed cuts to foreign aid from wealthy countries are likely to exacerbate the problem, particularly for those within developing countries.The UK intends to cut foreign aid spending from 0.5% to 0.3% of national income by the end of 2027. Worryingly, in its 2025-26 report, the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office proposed a cut of 35% on funding provided to the Democratic Republic of Congo. As your article pointed out, the DRC is already experiencing a deadly Ebola outbreak; with the spread of measles, thousands more will be lost to a different, and largely preventable disease. Continue reading...

items.standfirst: We point to self-care as we skip out on activities – but routinely staying home poses its own risk to our mental healthYou might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely, especially if they’re young.The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing.
